# Building a Community That Lasts: The Complete Guide

Source: https://lowob.com/research/building-a-community-that-lasts/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-15 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Growth

> Summary: Most company communities are audiences with a chat room, recruited for a payout and measured by headcount. This guide brings together lowob's research on community into one sequence: name what you have, give it a job, recruit the first hundred by hand, design the spaces and roles, treat incentives as acquisition costs, and measure contribution and retention after the money stops.

A community that lasts is a group of people doing a job together, with a reason to return that does not depend on being paid. Most company communities fail one of three tests: they are audiences rather than groups whose members create value for each other, they were recruited with incentives that selected for people who leave, or they are measured by member count, which says little about either. This guide sets out the sequence **lowob** recommends, from naming what you have to measuring who is still there after the incentives stop, and points to the article that covers each stage in depth.

## Why most communities do not last

Three findings explain most failures, and they come from different kinds of evidence.

**Participation is unequal by nature.** Jakob Nielsen's 2006 analysis of participation inequality described the 90-9-1 pattern: in most online communities about 90% of people read without contributing, 9% contribute occasionally and 1% produce most of the content. A 2014 observational study in the Journal of Medical Internet Research tested this in four digital health networks with 63,990 members. The top 1% wrote 74.7% of posts, the next 9% wrote 24.0% and the other 90% wrote 1.3%. Adding members mostly adds readers. A community lasts if its small active core lasts.

**Newcomers leave fast unless someone responds.** Kraut and colleagues' study of Usenet groups found 69% of newcomers left after their first day. By day 30, 31% of newcomers whose first post drew three or more replies were still participating, against 12% of those who got none. On English Wikipedia, Halfaker and colleagues found active editor numbers stopped growing in early 2007 and then declined, driven by falling retention of good-faith newcomers whose first edits were increasingly reverted. Groups that ignore or reject first contributions stop renewing themselves.

**Incentives select for people who leave.** In a study of nine major airdrops, Messias, Yaish and Livshits found up to 66% of tokens were sold soon after claiming in some cases, and concluded airdrops "may be necessary to attract users initially, but insufficient on their own". Two years after the Uniswap airdrop, Dune data showed 93% of recipients had sold all their UNI and about 98% had never voted in governance.

The field still counts heads. CMX's 2025 survey of 589 community professionals found the number of active members was the most used health metric, at 84%, and only 24% could confidently put a financial value on their community.

## Stage 1: Name what you have

An audience receives. A customer transacts. A user engages with a product. A network participant, such as a developer, liquidity provider or node operator, makes a shared system more useful. A community member participates in a group whose value is partly created by other members. One person can be all of these, but the strategies differ.

The quickest test is the peer-value test: remove the company for a week and see whether members still help each other, share knowledge and organise. If activity stops, the company has an audience or a support channel. That is not a failure. The mistake is designing for one group while measuring another.

The test can also be run on data. Common Room's 2022 analysis of 141 communities (vendor research) found members replied to each other 28% of the time outside GitHub, against 13% for staff. Where staff answer everything, the community is a help desk.

Some companies should stop here: products that need onboarding and support more than peer relationships should invest in those. Our piece on [audience vs community](https://lowob.com/research/community-vs-audience/) sets out the four groups, the "members return because" sentence and when not to build a community at all.

## Stage 2: Give it a job

A community earns its keep by doing work the company would otherwise pay for. **lowob**'s framework names five jobs:

| Job | What members do | Contribution measure |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Test | Use early builds, report bugs, give feedback | Bugs found, release sign-offs |
| Teach | Answer questions, write guides, onboard newcomers | Share of questions answered by members |
| Refer | Bring customers, partners or hires | Referred sign-ups and their conversion |
| Build | Integrate, extend, ship on top of you | Integrations and plugins in use |
| Govern | Make decisions with real consequences | Participation by people who are not whales or the team |

Pick one or two. A community asked to do all five does none of them well.

Governance needs particular care in crypto. A 2024 study of Aave, Compound, Lido and Uniswap found only about 5% of tokens were cast on a typical proposal and the top three or four holders could decide almost every vote. Counting the largest wallets measures concentration, not community.

The job also protects against platform risk. On 15 January 2026, X revoked API access for apps that paid users to post, and The Block reported the KAITO token fell 14.5% that day. [Community is a job, not a number](https://lowob.com/research/community-is-a-job-not-a-number/) covers the design choices that follow from each job: channel, rituals, recognition and ownership of the record.

> Silence is the correct response to no job. A community with nothing to do will do nothing, however many people are in it.

## Stage 3: Recruit and run the first hundred

The first hundred community members are recruited, not attracted. Paul Graham's essay "Do Things That Don't Scale" makes the general point for start-ups: "The most common unscalable thing founders have to do at the start is to recruit users manually."

**lowob** splits this stage across two pieces.

**[The first hundred](https://lowob.com/research/the-first-hundred/) covers recruitment.** List 30 names: potential customers, respected builders, operators and sharp critics. Ask each for judgment on a real decision rather than attention. Give those who say yes a job with an end date. Close the loop in public, so they can see what changed because of them. Ask each for the next name. Because participation is unequal, the aim is to get the people who will do most of the work into the first hundred.

**[Find your first 100 people who actually care](https://lowob.com/research/first-100-community-members/) covers operation.** Define an active member by behaviour (answering a question, testing the product, creating a resource, returning over several weeks) rather than by joining. Write a narrow member thesis. Start with one recurring ritual, such as a weekly teardown or an integration clinic, and make sure every newcomer's first question gets answered, which is what the Kraut findings point to. Give members consequential roles, run a weekly member-health review and invite the next cohort only when the first is getting consistent value. Growth through density beats growth through size: Common Room found engagement rates of 2% to 12% across surfaces, highest in smaller communities.

Kraut and Resnick's *Building Successful Online Communities* (MIT Press) turns the research behind this stage into design claims on contribution and commitment.

For media businesses, the first hundred are the hundred readers whose job titles you would put in a sponsor deck. [Membership is the job](https://lowob.com/research/membership-is-the-job/) applies the same recruitment by name to paid membership, where the market is tight: the Reuters Institute's 2026 Digital News Report found 17% of people across 20 paywall-heavy markets paid for online news.

## Stage 4: Design the spaces and staff them

Opening a Discord or Telegram is one of the fastest ways for a project to feel operational. The interface resembles a community before the relationships exist. [Discord is not a community strategy. Neither is Telegram.](https://lowob.com/research/discord-telegram-community-strategy/) argues for starting with the jobs members need the environment to do, then building a small architecture: a start-here space with rules and security warnings, read-only announcements, structured help, one or two discussion spaces, a contribute space and events.

Platform metrics help if read correctly. Discord's Server Insights tracks visitors, communicators who post, and the share of new members who return after a week, and suggests about 30% communicators as a healthy goal. These measure presence, not whether the job is getting done.

Staffing follows from the same logic. [Community management vs social media management](https://lowob.com/research/community-vs-social-media-management/) sets out why they are different jobs. Social media management is editorial: the company's voice on its accounts. Community management is hosting: members' voices in the company's spaces. Combining them by default means one gets neglected, and which one depends on the person's temperament rather than the company's needs. The resourcing gap is real: CMX found 17% of organisations had no one working full time on community, the highest share it had recorded.

## Stage 5: Use incentives as acquisition costs

Incentives can overcome a cold start, distribute ownership and reward early users. They also redefine what participation means. If a project rewards transaction count, participants maximise transactions; if it rewards posting, they maximise posts. [Airdrops can buy attention. They cannot buy belief.](https://lowob.com/research/airdrops-points-community-incentives/) sets out the questions to answer before launching any incentive: the behaviour being rewarded, the durable value it creates, how it can be farmed and what happens when the reward ends.

The evidence on airdrops is consistent. Beyond the Messias and Dune findings above, Keyrock, a crypto market maker, reviewed 62 airdrops in 2024 and found only eight trading above their launch price after 90 days, with larger distributions holding up better than small ones.

[Community that survives the airdrop](https://lowob.com/research/community-that-survives-the-airdrop/) turns this into a plan. Treat the airdrop as an acquisition cost with an expected sell-through. Weight allocation to repeated usage over time. Build sybil filters before the snapshot, publish the rules and keep an appeals channel a human reads. Give holders a job: test, curate, govern or refer.

Paid creators are the same problem in a different channel. [KOL campaigns need more than impression screenshots](https://lowob.com/research/web3-kol-campaign-measurement/) argues for defining the action before buying placements and judging spend by cost per activated, retained user rather than reach. For the wider cost logic, see [demand generation economics](https://lowob.com/research/demand-generation-economics/).

## Stage 6: Measure contribution and retention

Member count is the easiest number to inflate and one of the weakest indicators of health. Replace it with measures that match the job and show whether people stay.

| Measure | What it shows | Where it fits |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Meaningful first contributions by newcomers | Whether people move past reading | Every community |
| Time to a useful response | Whether newcomers are being answered | Every community; critical in the first hundred |
| Share of questions answered by members | Peer value exists | Teach job |
| Distinct contributors per month | Breadth of the active core | Every community |
| Contribution to the chosen job | Bugs, referrals, integrations, guides | Test, refer, build, teach |
| Governance participation excluding the largest holders and team | Real distribution of decisions | Govern job |
| Retained usage 30 days after incentives stop | The community that remains | Any incentive programme |
| Member retention and paid revenue from referring members | Whether peer value funds the business | Media memberships |

The single most important line is the retained-usage figure. Define the action that means someone is using the product, not visiting it. Run incentives for a set period, stop, and count how many keep doing it. Write the decision you will make on the result before you start; [campaign testing that reaches a decision](https://lowob.com/research/campaign-testing-that-reaches-a-decision/) covers how. Keep that record, a member list, a contribution log and a way to reach people, on systems you own, so a platform policy change cannot take it.

## When it has gone wrong

A large, silent group was usually recruited for a payout, lives on a rented platform and shares only an interest in price or launch news. Some silence is normal, but a large group with no active core has a design problem. ["40,000 members and nobody does anything"](https://lowob.com/research/40-000-members-and-nobody-does-anything/) sets out the turnaround: pick one job, hand-recruit thirty people from the channel history who asked real questions or helped others, ask them for judgment on a real decision, close the loop in public, switch incentives off for a month and count who stays. Do not buy more members or announce a token to wake the group up.

## lowob takeaways

- **Name the group.** Run the peer-value test before calling anything a community.
- **Assign one or two jobs.** Test, teach, refer, build or govern, each with its own contribution measure.
- **Recruit the first hundred by hand.** Ask for judgment, close the loop and answer every first contribution.
- **Design small and host it.** A few spaces with clear jobs, run by a host rather than a publisher.
- **Cost the incentives.** Airdrops, points and paid creators are acquisition spend with an expected loss rate.
- **Count who stays.** Retained contribution after incentives stop is the community.

Gateway card

### Before you call it a community

- You can complete "members return because they can \_\_\_ with people they could not easily \_\_\_ elsewhere"
- One or two named jobs, each with a contribution measure
- A named first hundred, recruited by hand, with a record of each person's first contribution
- One recurring ritual and a host responsible for answering newcomers
- Every incentive costed, with a date it stops and a retained-usage count planned
- Member records held on systems you own

Working paper; Usenet groups; behavioural measures.

- [Halfaker, Geiger, Morgan and Riedl, The Rise and Decline of an Open Collaboration System, summary on Wikimedia Meta](https://meta.wikimedia.org/wiki/Research:The_Rise_and_Decline), 2013. Published in American Behavioral Scientist; English Wikipedia only.

- [Discord, Getting to Know Your Server With Server Insights](https://discord.com/community/understanding-server-insights), undated. Platform documentation.
- [Messias, Yaish and Livshits, Airdrops: Giving Money Away Is Harder Than It Seems, arXiv](https://arxiv.org/html/2312.02752v4), revised July 2025. Academic preprint; nine airdrops.
